name: Main-sequence star
summary: Stars like the Sun that fuse hydrogen into helium in their cores, about 90% of a star's life.
how: Gravity squeezes the core to ~15 million K, where hydrogen fuses; outward radiation pressure balances gravity in hydrostatic equilibrium.
evidence: The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram; helioseismology of the Sun.

name: Red dwarf
summary: The most common stars in the galaxy (~75%), small, cool and able to shine for trillions of years.
how: Low mass (0.08–0.6 Sun) means slow fusion and fully convective interiors that mix fuel.
evidence: Proxima Centauri, TRAPPIST-1; frequent flares challenge habitability of their planets.

name: Brown dwarf
summary: 'Failed stars' between ~13 and ~80 Jupiter masses that never sustain hydrogen fusion.
how: Too light to fuse ordinary hydrogen; they briefly burn deuterium and then cool for ever.
evidence: First confirmed in 1995 (Gliese 229B, Teide 1); WISE found the coldest, near room temperature.

name: Red giant
summary: What Sun-like stars become when core hydrogen runs out: swollen to hundreds of times their size.
how: The core contracts and heats while a hydrogen-burning shell inflates the outer layers; later helium ignites in a 'helium flash'.
evidence: Arcturus, Aldebaran; the Sun will become one in ~5 billion years.

name: Supergiant and hypergiant
summary: The largest and most luminous stars, destined to explode.
how: Massive stars (>8 Suns) fuse heavier elements in shells like an onion up to iron.
evidence: Betelgeuse, Rigel, UY Scuti, Eta Carinae.

name: White dwarf
summary: The hot, Earth-sized remnant core of a Sun-like star, supported by electron degeneracy pressure.
how: After a red giant sheds a planetary nebula, the exposed core (mostly carbon and oxygen) slowly cools; maximum mass ~1.4 Suns (Chandrasekhar limit).
evidence: Sirius B; ~97% of all stars will end this way.

name: Black dwarf
summary: A white dwarf cooled until it no longer glows, which takes far longer than the universe's current age.
how: Cooling over ~10¹⁵ years.
evidence: None exist yet: the universe is only 13.8 billion years old.

name: Neutron star
summary: The collapsed core of a massive star: more mass than the Sun packed into a city-sized ball ~20 km across.
how: In a core-collapse supernova, electrons and protons merge into neutrons; neutron degeneracy halts the collapse.
evidence: A teaspoon weighs ~a billion tonnes; NICER measures their sizes.

name: Pulsar
summary: A spinning neutron star sweeping radio beams across Earth like a lighthouse.
how: Strong magnetic fields channel radiation from the poles; rotation makes it pulse.
evidence: Discovered by Jocelyn Bell Burnell in 1967; millisecond pulsars spin over 700 times a second.

name: Magnetar
summary: Neutron stars with the strongest magnetic fields in the universe (~10¹⁵ gauss).
how: Decaying magnetic fields crack the crust, releasing giant flares; linked to some fast radio bursts.
evidence: SGR 1806-20's 2004 giant flare; SGR 1935+2154 produced a fast radio burst in 2020.

name: Variable star (Cepheid)
summary: Pulsating stars whose period reveals their true brightness, used as cosmic distance markers.
how: Layers of ionised helium trap and release heat, driving pulsations.
evidence: Henrietta Leavitt's 1912 period–luminosity law let Hubble measure distances to galaxies.

name: Wolf–Rayet star
summary: Hot, massive stars stripping off their own outer layers in violent winds.
how: Intense radiation drives winds that expose helium-, carbon- or nitrogen-rich layers.
evidence: WR 104, WR 140 dust shells imaged by JWST.

name: Supernova (core-collapse)
summary: The explosion of a massive star whose iron core collapses in under a second.
how: Iron cannot release energy by fusion; the core collapses into a neutron star or black hole and the rebound plus neutrinos blow the star apart.
evidence: SN 1987A in the Large Magellanic Cloud, the first detected by neutrinos; it forged and scattered elements like oxygen and calcium.

name: Type Ia supernova
summary: A white dwarf exploding after gaining too much mass, a 'standard candle' that revealed dark energy.
how: Accretion from a companion or a white-dwarf merger triggers runaway carbon fusion.
evidence: 1998 discovery of the accelerating universe (Nobel Prize 2011).

name: Kilonova
summary: The explosion when two neutron stars merge, forging gold, platinum and other heavy elements.
how: Rapid neutron capture (r-process) in ejected neutron-rich matter.
evidence: GW170817 (2017): gravitational waves plus light from the same event, first multi-messenger observation.

name: Gamma-ray burst
summary: The most energetic explosions known, flashes of gamma rays lasting milliseconds to minutes.
how: Long bursts come from collapsing massive stars (collapsars); short bursts from neutron star mergers.
evidence: GRB 221009A (2022), the 'BOAT', brightest of all time.

name: Nova
summary: A white dwarf flaring as hydrogen from a companion ignites on its surface.
how: Thermonuclear runaway on the surface; the star survives and can repeat.
evidence: T Coronae Borealis, a recurrent nova, was expected to erupt in 2024–26.

name: Stellar collision
summary: Stars actually crashing together, common only in dense star clusters.
how: In globular cluster cores, close encounters merge stars into 'blue stragglers'.
evidence: V1309 Scorpii (2008) was seen merging as a 'red nova'.

name: Galaxy collision
summary: Galaxies merge over hundreds of millions of years; stars rarely touch but gas collapses into new stars.
how: Gravity pulls galaxies together; tidal forces fling out streams of stars.
evidence: The Antennae galaxies; the Milky Way and Andromeda will merge in ~4–5 billion years (a 2025 study put the odds near 50%).

name: Black hole merger
summary: Two black holes spiralling together and releasing more power than all the stars in the universe, as gravitational waves.
how: Orbital energy is radiated as ripples in spacetime until the horizons merge and 'ring down'.
evidence: GW150914 (first detection, 2015); GW250114 confirmed Hawking's area law at ~99.999% confidence.

name: Fast radio burst
summary: Millisecond flashes of radio waves from distant galaxies.
how: Many likely come from magnetars.
evidence: First found in 2007; CHIME detects them daily; FRB 20200428 came from a Milky Way magnetar.

name: Black hole
summary: A region where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape.
how: Forms when matter collapses within its Schwarzschild radius; the boundary is the event horizon; general relativity predicts a singularity inside.
evidence: X-ray binaries (Cygnus X-1), stars orbiting Sgr A* (Nobel 2020), gravitational waves, Event Horizon Telescope images (M87* 2019, Sgr A* 2022).

name: Stellar-mass black hole
summary: Black holes of a few to ~100 solar masses left by dead massive stars.
how: Core collapse of stars above ~20–25 Suns.
evidence: Gaia BH3 (33 Suns), the most massive in the Milky Way.

name: Supermassive black hole
summary: Monsters of millions to billions of solar masses at the centres of galaxies.
how: Grow by accreting gas and merging; how the first ones grew so fast is a major puzzle.
evidence: Sgr A* (4.3 million Suns); M87* (6.5 billion); JWST finds them less than 500 million years after the Big Bang.

name: Intermediate-mass black hole
summary: Missing-link black holes of ~100 to 100,000 Suns.
how: May form in dense clusters by runaway mergers.
evidence: Fast-moving stars in Omega Centauri (2024) revealed one of at least ~8,200 Suns; GW190521 produced a ~142-Sun remnant.

name: Primordial black hole
summary: Hypothetical black holes formed in the first second after the Big Bang; a dark-matter candidate.
how: Dense fluctuations in the early universe could collapse directly.
evidence: No confirmed detection; microlensing surveys constrain them.

name: Hawking radiation
summary: Stephen Hawking's 1974 prediction that black holes slowly evaporate by emitting radiation.
how: Quantum effects near the horizon cause a faint thermal glow; tiny black holes evaporate fastest.
evidence: Not observed directly (far too faint); analogues seen in lab experiments.

name: Accretion disk and jets
summary: Swirling gas around black holes, heated to millions of degrees, launching jets at nearly light speed.
how: Friction and magnetic fields heat infalling matter; spin and magnetic fields launch jets.
evidence: M87's 5,000-light-year jet; quasars outshine entire galaxies.

name: Quasar
summary: The brightest objects in the universe: supermassive black holes feeding voraciously.
how: Gas falling into a black hole radiates intensely before crossing the horizon.
evidence: 3C 273 identified in 1963; the most distant seen at z>7.

name: White hole
summary: The time-reverse of a black hole: a region that nothing can enter but from which matter and light pour out.
how: A valid mathematical solution of Einstein's equations (the extended Schwarzschild spacetime), but unstable; some speculate black holes may end as white holes or that the Big Bang was one.
evidence: No observational evidence.

name: Wormhole
summary: A hypothetical tunnel through spacetime linking distant places or times (an Einstein–Rosen bridge).
how: Allowed by general relativity, but keeping one open would need 'exotic matter' with negative energy; quantum effects may forbid it.
evidence: No evidence; studied in theory and quantum-gravity 'ER = EPR' ideas.

name: Gravitational waves
summary: Ripples in spacetime predicted by Einstein in 1916 and first detected in 2015.
how: Accelerating masses, especially merging black holes and neutron stars, stretch and squeeze space as waves travel at light speed.
evidence: LIGO–Virgo–KAGRA have detected ~300 events; pulsar timing arrays found a background hum (2023). Nobel Prize 2017.

name: Gravitational lensing
summary: Massive objects bend light, magnifying and distorting background galaxies.
how: Mass curves spacetime, so light follows curved paths.
evidence: Eddington's 1919 eclipse confirmed general relativity; lensing magnified Earendel.

name: Spaghettification
summary: Being stretched into a noodle by tidal forces near a black hole.
how: Gravity pulls harder on the near end of an object than the far end.
evidence: Tidal disruption events show stars shredded by black holes.

name: Cosmic microwave background
summary: The afterglow of the Big Bang, light released 380,000 years after it began.
how: When the universe cooled to ~3,000 K, atoms formed and light travelled freely; expansion stretched it to microwaves (2.7 K).
evidence: Discovered by Penzias and Wilson (1965); mapped by COBE, WMAP and Planck.

name: Dark matter
summary: Invisible matter making up ~85% of all matter, revealed only by its gravity.
how: Unknown particles (or other forms) that do not interact with light.
evidence: Galaxy rotation curves (Vera Rubin), the Bullet Cluster, CMB patterns, lensing.

name: Dark energy
summary: The mysterious cause of the accelerating expansion, ~68% of the universe's energy.
how: Possibly a cosmological constant; DESI (2025) hinted it may evolve over time.
evidence: Supernova surveys (1998), BAO, CMB.

name: Cosmic void
summary: Vast near-empty regions between galaxy filaments, up to hundreds of millions of light-years across.
how: Matter flowed out of underdense regions into filaments and clusters.
evidence: The Boötes Void (~330 million light-years across); the KBC void may surround the Milky Way.

name: The vacuum of space
summary: Space is not perfectly empty: intergalactic space holds about one atom per cubic metre.
how: Even 'empty' space has the CMB, neutrinos, magnetic fields and quantum vacuum fluctuations.
evidence: Interstellar medium ~1 atom/cm³; Casimir effect shows vacuum energy.

name: Cosmic web
summary: The large-scale structure of the universe: filaments, walls and nodes of galaxies around voids.
how: Dark matter clumps grew from tiny fluctuations, pulling galaxies into a web.
evidence: Galaxy redshift surveys (SDSS, DESI); filaments imaged directly in 2023–24.

name: Cosmic rays
summary: High-energy particles from space, mostly protons, some with energies far beyond human accelerators.
how: Accelerated by supernova shocks and active galaxies.
evidence: The 'Oh-My-God' particle (1991) and 'Amaterasu' (2023).

name: Nebula
summary: Clouds of gas and dust where stars are born or have died.
how: Emission nebulae glow from ionised gas; dark nebulae block light; planetary nebulae and supernova remnants are stellar deaths.
evidence: Orion Nebula, Pillars of Creation, Crab Nebula.

name: Stardust (cosmic dust)
summary: Tiny grains of silicate and carbon forged in dying stars, the raw material of planets and of us.
how: Condense in cool outflows of giant stars and supernova ejecta.
evidence: Presolar grains in meteorites; Stardust mission returned comet dust (2006); interstellar dust collected.
